title: Bouldering fall onto ribs with worsening breathing

source.title: Case Study: Chest Injury with Fall

classification.acuity_basis: Shortness of breath with worsening HR/RR and pale clammy skin; 911 and assisted walk-out to EMS.

context.distance_to_care: cell service at parking area; EMS met group on walk-out

presentation.summary: Climber's hand slips and she falls about 10 ft onto her right side. Bystander WFR finds her on her side with right rib pain and shortness of breath.
exam_findings: bruising and tenderness right rib cage

plan: full assessment then focused spine assessment
position of comfort, monitor breathing, encourage deep breaths
teaching_points: Rib fracture signs: point tenderness, splinting, pain on inspiration, shallow breathing.
Lung injury signs: SOB at rest, chest wall instability, rising HR/RR, pale cool clammy skin.
Worsening: respiratory distress, crackling under skin, diminished breath sounds one side, cyanosis, distended neck veins, tracheal shift.
Care: stabilize, position of comfort, seal open wounds, consider sling and swathe, deep breaths; evacuate if SOB increases.

decision_points.question: Evacuate?
decision_points.source_decision: Yes, call 911 and move toward road

outcome.summary: Friend called 911 from parking area; EMS met the group en route.

must_ask: is the pain worse when breathing in?
eval.must_escalate: Call EMS for chest injury with shortness of breath, especially if worsening.

lay_queries: fell on my side and it hurts to breathe
my friend fell climbing and is breathing fast and getting pale
red_flags: shortness of breath after chest trauma

title: Accidental bear spray discharge into the face

source.title: Case Study: Bear Spray in the Face

classification.acuity_basis: Symptoms resolved with irrigation; walked out 1 mile.

presentation.summary: While taking off a pack, a bear spray canister catches on the hip belt, the safety pops and it discharges into the hiker's face.
exam_findings: red irritated eyes, hard to examine, PERRL

assessment: eye and face exposure to bear spray
plan: move upwind out of contaminated area
irrigate copiously with cool clean water
monitor for airway or systemic signs
teaching_points: Capsaicin binds skin and mucous membranes causing intense burning.
Use cool water; warm water worsens it.
Usually resolves within hours; seek care if persistent or allergic signs.
Prevention: keep safety on, careful pack handling.

decision_points.question: Walk out?
decision_points.source_decision: Yes once able to see and stand, following creek for more irrigation

outcome.summary: Partial eye opening after 45 min irrigation, walking after 20 more min; hiked 1 mi out.

must_recognize: chemical eye exposure needs prolonged irrigation
must_ask: any trouble breathing or throat swelling?
eval.must_escalate: Seek care if breathing problems, vision doesn't recover, or symptoms persist.
must_not_recommend: milk as primary irrigant over water

lay_queries: I sprayed bear spray in my face
pepper spray in eyes what do I do

title: Unacclimatized wildland firefighter with dizziness and nausea

source.title: Case Study: Heat Illness on an Early-Season Wildland Fire Assignment

classification.acuity_basis: Normal mental status; improved in 30-45 min with cooling and fluids.

context.weather: mid-80s F, full sun, intermittent smoke

presentation.summary: Mid-afternoon on an early-season fire assignment, a crew member gradually becomes dizzy, nauseated and fatigued after hours of line digging on a sunny slope. Drank only ~1 L.
presentation.last_intake_output: ~1 L water over several hours; one dark yellow urination

plan: stop work, shade, remove pack, loosen clothing
active cooling with airflow and water on skin
teaching_points: Early-season heat illness is common before acclimatization.
Stimulant medications raise heat risk.
Dizziness, nausea, fatigue and rising HR call for immediate rest and cooling.
Watch for confusion and loss of sweating.

outcome.summary: Improved after 30-45 min; rejoined crew on lighter duty; no recurrence.

must_ask: how much have you drunk and what color is your urine?
eval.must_escalate: Rapid cooling and evacuation if confusion or collapse.

lay_queries: working on a fire line and feel dizzy and sick
overheated and nauseous digging in the sun

title: Early non-freezing cold injury of the feet on a canoe trip

source.title: Case Study: Non-Freezing Cold Injury on a Canoe Trip

classification.acuity_basis: Early NFCI improved over 24-48 h with drying and modified travel.

context.weather: mid-May, mild air, very cold water

presentation.summary: After a day of wading in and out of cold water at portages, a paddler has gradually numb, tingling, uncomfortable feet. In camp feet are pale, cool, mildly swollen and wrinkled.
exam_findings: feet pale, cool, mildly swollen, macerated

plan: remove wet footwear, dry feet gently
gradual rewarming with dry socks and body heat (not aggressive)
dry sock rotation, limit standing in water
teaching_points: NFCI happens above freezing with prolonged cold wet exposure.
Early signs: numbness, tingling, pale or swollen skin.
Gentle rewarming; avoid rapid heat.
Prevention: dry feet, sock changes, limit immersion.

must_ask: how long have your feet been wet?
eval.must_escalate: Evacuate if pain, swelling, color change or inability to walk progresses.

lay_queries: feet numb and wrinkly after wading all day
my feet tingle after being wet all day canoeing

title: Persistent vomiting from motion sickness on a dive boat

source.title: Case Study: Motion Sickness on a Surf and Dive Trip in Oahu, Hawaii

presentation.summary: Nausea starts on a curvy coastal drive, eases on land, then returns worse on a dive boat with repeated vomiting.

assessment: consider GI illness or pregnancy if persists off motion
plan: stable spot with horizon view, fresh air
anticipated_problems: underlying illness if persists on land
teaching_points: Motion sickness can become a safety issue in water activities.
Simple measures help but not always; adjust objectives.
Persisting symptoms off motion suggest another cause.

outcome.summary: Better on land; stayed ashore next day; resolved.

must_recognize: motion sickness vs other causes of vomiting
must_ask: does it stop when you're on land?
eval.must_escalate: Seek care if vomiting persists on land or signs of dehydration.

nauseous on the boat what helps

title: Tooth knocked out by paddle T-grip on a river trip

source.title: Case Study: Dental Emergency while Rafting

classification.acuity_basis: Avulsed tooth; dental care next day.

context.distance_to_care: next day to car, dentist by early afternoon

presentation.summary: Rafter hits his mouth with his own paddle's T-grip in a rapid and loses a front tooth.
presentation.chief_complaint: I think I lost a tooth

plan: if not, store and evacuate to dentist
teaching_points: Reimplantation becomes hard after ~30 min.
Rinse with drinkable water; don't scrub the root.
Storage: balanced salt solution > milk > saliva.
Analgesics for pain; evacuate for dental care.

outcome.summary: Tooth stored in milk; planned exit next morning to dentist.

must_ask: any other head or face injury?
eval.must_escalate: Dental care as soon as possible.
must_not_recommend: storing tooth dry or in plain water long term

lay_queries: I knocked my tooth out what do I do
tooth fell out after getting hit with a paddle

title: Tumbling fall onto rocks on a kayak break: deformed wrist

classification.acuity_basis: Unusable deformed wrist; spine cleared; paddled out in double kayak to clinic.

context.distance_to_care: several hours paddling then drive to clinic

presentation.summary: During a beach break a paddler slips descending a small hill and tumbles about 12 ft onto rocks. Found on her back with right wrist pain.
exam_findings: right wrist deformity, redness, reduced motion, weak grip
pertinent_negatives: CSM intact in legs and left hand

plan: splint unusable wrist (padded, rigid, immobilize joints above and below)
anticipated_problems: unusable wrist or spine injury needs more help to exit
teaching_points: Complete the full assessment before focused spine exam.
Splint: padded, rigid, adjustable, allows CSM checks, immobilizes joints above and below.
Carry a kit and field guide even on day trips.

decision_points.question: Can she paddle?
decision_points.source_decision: Ride as passenger in double kayak

outcome.summary: Splinted with sit pad; paddled out as passenger; clinic visit.

must_ask: can you move fingers and feel them?
must_not_recommend: having her paddle with the injured wrist

lay_queries: I fell and my wrist looks bent
how do I splint a broken wrist with what I have

title: Surfer stung on the arm by a jellyfish

source.title: Case Study: Jellyfish Sting in Paradise

classification.acuity_basis: Local symptoms only; eased with hot water soak.

presentation.summary: While paddling out a surfer feels stinging pain on her right arm after suspected jellyfish contact.
exam_findings: red-brown spots and swelling right arm

teaching_points: Don't scrape, rub, or rinse with fresh water (can fire more stingers).
Heat inactivates venom: ~41C for 30-90 min.
Vinegar helps box jellyfish but may worsen other species.
Evacuate if pain persists, rash spreads, systemic illness, or infection signs.

outcome.summary: Pain eased after 30 min soak; monitor, clinic if persistent.

must_recognize: marine envenomation; watch for systemic reaction
must_ask: any trouble breathing, chest pain, or widespread rash?
what kind of jellyfish / where are you?
eval.must_escalate: Emergency care for breathing difficulty, collapse, or box jellyfish regions.

title: Climber bitten on the forearm by a snake after a short fall

source.title: Caso de Estudio 06: Mordedura de Serpiente (Spanish)

classification.acuity_basis: All snakebites evacuated; progressive swelling and pain en route; antivenom given.

context.distance_to_care: 5 min walk to road, drive to town hospital

presentation.summary: Climber falls, hits helmeted head and rolls once, and is bitten on the right forearm. Two punctures 2 cm apart, one oozing blood-tinged fluid.

plan: splint and immobilize arm at heart level
anticipated_problems: envenomation: increasing pain, bruising, swelling, loss of CSM
teaching_points: Most North American envenomations are pit vipers; antivenom is the treatment.
Pit viper signs: pain and swelling within ~30 min, later bruising/blisters, nausea, numbness, sweating.
30-50% of bites are dry, but evacuate all bites; rapidly if signs of envenomation.
Don't catch or kill the snake.
No tourniquet, ice, electricity, incision, or suction; avoid constriction; avoid aspirin.
Pressure immobilization is for elapids (e.g. coral snake, Australian snakes), not pit vipers.

outcome.summary: Swelling and pain increased en route; at ED tingling throughout arm and bruising around punctures; antivenom given.

must_ask: rings or watches on that arm?
eval.must_escalate: Evacuate every snakebite to a hospital; urgently if swelling spreads.

lay_queries: I just got bitten by a rattlesnake

should I suck out snake venom

title: Skier breaks through lake ice: cold water immersion and mild hypothermia

classification.acuity_basis: Alert and shivering; rewarmed in <1 h with hypothermia wrap; trip continued.

presentation.summary: Crossing a lake despite agreeing not to, a skier breaks through the ice about 20 m from shore and self-rescues after 5-10 minutes. Clothing freezes quickly; shivering violently.
exam_findings: fingers and toes cold, not frozen

assessment: mild hypothermia; at risk of severe hypothermia and frostbite
plan: replace wet with dry clothing including hat, gloves, socks
teaching_points: Cold water: control the gasp in the first minute, ~10 min of useful movement, ~1 h before severe hypothermia.
Hypothermia wrap: dry insulation inside a vapor barrier; if wet clothes can't come off, put barrier between wet clothes and insulation.
Warm sweet drinks fuel shivering but barely warm the core.
A second person in the bag adds little heat; better to make hot bottles and food.
Fed, hydrated patients rewarm better.

outcome.summary: Shivering eased, felt warm in under an hour; continued trip next day.
outcome.final_diagnosis: mild hypothermia after cold water immersion

must_ask: is he shivering and talking normally?
do you have dry clothes and a sleeping bag?
how long was he in the water?
eval.must_escalate: Evacuate if shivering stops with confusion or drowsiness.
must_not_recommend: vigorous exercise to warm if impaired

lay_queries: my friend fell through the ice and is soaked and shaking
what to do after falling in freezing water

provenance.notes: Translated from Spanish source; paraphrased facts only. Source notes inconsistency about submersion depth.

title: Lethargic 42-year-old on day 1 of a high trek: altitude, exhaustion or diabetes?

classification.acuity_basis: Lethargic, unable to continue; descended and horse-evacuated.

context.weather: late August, icy, wet, low clouds, snow patches
context.distance_to_care: 6.5 km to trailhead then drive to phone

presentation.summary: Found lethargic in a tent in wet clothes and a wet sleeping bag after flying from sea level two days earlier and crossing a 3,400 m pass in wet snow. Slow to respond but oriented.
presentation.last_intake_output: ~3 L yesterday, a cup or two today, no dinner, yellow urine
presentation.events_leading_up: sea level -> 1500 m -> 2400 m same day; next day 10 km over >3400 m pass, camp 3000 m

plan: warm dry clothing, food and fluids
if no improvement send two for help
teaching_points: Differential: exhaustion, dehydration, AMS, diabetic complication, inability to cope.
Descent is a key intervention if altitude illness is possible.
Simple care (dry, warm, fed) plus leadership matters.

outcome.summary: Descended ~500 m over 3 h, then exhausted; horses carried patient to trailhead where he looked much better.

must_ask: how fast did you go up?
eval.must_escalate: Descend; evacuate if no improvement or mental status worsens.

lay_queries: friend is super tired and slow after flying in and hiking high
really weak first day at altitude

provenance.notes: Translated from Spanish source (event early 1980s); paraphrased facts only.

title: Canoeist with leg cramps mistaken for a seizure on the Rio Grande

source.title: Caso de Estudio 11: Calambre por Calor (Spanish); English version 'Heat Cramps on the Rio Grande'

classification.acuity_basis: Normal mental status, 37.2C; cramps resolved with stretching, cooling, electrolytes.

context.region: Rio Grande, Big Bend NP, Texas

presentation.summary: Kneeling in a canoe after a long hot hike, a participant develops painful leg spasms; bystanders think it's a seizure. He is awake, oriented, crying in pain.
symptoms: later hand cramps and rapid breathing
presentation.last_intake_output: 3 L water today and yesterday; no food today

teaching_points: Rule out seizure: patient stays awake and responsive with cramp-like movements.
Check temperature and mental status to rule out heat stroke.
Cramps relate to salt/electrolyte loss with low food intake.
Gentle stretching relieves cramps.

outcome.summary: Cramps eased over 30 min; walking and fine by dusk; no evacuation.

must_ask: is he awake and talking during the spasms?
eval.must_escalate: Rapid cooling and evacuation if confusion or temp >40C.
must_not_recommend: plain water only in large amounts with no food

lay_queries: his legs are cramping badly in the heat
muscle spasms is it a seizure

provenance.notes: Translated from Spanish source; paraphrased. English version published 2024-05-14 at nols.edu/blog/case-study-heat-cramps-on-the-rio-grande/. Salt quantity for oral solution omitted pending verification.
